#739. Exercise doesn't just strengthen your heart. It rewires it

Exercise does more than make the heart stronger. New research suggests it also physically reshapes the nerves that control the heart, revealing an unexpected difference between the left and right sides of the body.

Scientists at the University of Bristol (UK) discovered that moderate aerobic exercise changes the structure of nerve cells involved in regulating heart activity. Even more surprisingly, the changes were dramatically different on the two sides of the body. The findings, published in Autonomic Neuroscience, could eventually help doctors develop more precise treatments for irregular heartbeats, chest pain, angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.

The discovery was made in rats, so further research is needed to determine whether the same changes occur in humans. Nevertheless, it offers a new perspective on how physical activity influences the nervous system that keeps the heart functioning.

Exercise Changes the Heart's Hidden Control System

The heart is regulated partly by the autonomic nervous system, a network of nerves that automatically manages essential functions such as heartbeat, breathing, and digestion. One branch of this system helps the heart beat faster when the body needs more oxygen, such as during exercise or stressful situations.

Small clusters of nerve cells called stellate ganglia play an important role in this process. Located on both sides of the lower neck and upper chest, these nerve hubs send signals that influence heart rate and other aspects of heart function.

The new research suggests that regular exercise changes these nerve clusters in ways scientists had not previously recognized.

Study lead author Dr. Augusto Coppi, Senior Lecturer in Veterinary Anatomy at the University of Bristol, said: "The discovery points to a previously hidden left-right pattern in the body's 'autopilot' system that helps run the heart.

"These nerve clusters act like the heart's dimmer switch and we've shown that regular, moderate exercise remodels that switch in a side-specific way. This could help explain why some treatments work better on one side than the other and, in future, help doctors target therapies more precisely and effectively."

Just 10 Weeks of Exercise Produced Striking Nerve Changes

To investigate how exercise affects these nerve clusters, the researchers examined rats that underwent 10 weeks of moderate aerobic training. Aerobic exercise is physical activity that increases heart rate and breathing, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling.

The study involved researchers from University College London (UCL) in the UK, the University of São Paulo (USP), and the Federal University of São Paulo (UNIFESP) in Brazil.

The team used advanced three-dimensional analysis techniques known as stereology to examine the nerve cells. This approach allows scientists to estimate the number, size, and distribution of cells within tissues.

The results revealed an unusual imbalance between the two sides of the body. In the trained rats, the cardiovascular nerve cluster on the right contained roughly four times as many neurons as the cluster on the left, a striking difference from the pattern observed in untrained rats.

The nerve cells also changed in size, but in opposite directions. Neurons on the left nearly doubled in size, while those on the right became slightly smaller.

These findings suggest that exercise does not affect all the nerves controlling the heart equally. Instead, it produces distinct structural changes on each side, potentially providing clues about how the nervous system adapts to regular physical activity.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Treatments?

The findings may have important implications for treating conditions involving abnormal nerve activity around the heart.

Arrhythmias occur when the heart beats too quickly, too slowly, or irregularly. Angina is chest pain or discomfort typically caused by insufficient blood flow to the heart muscle. Another condition, commonly called 'broken-heart' syndrome, involves a sudden weakening of the heart muscle that is often triggered by intense emotional or physical stress.

In some patients, doctors treat these problems by reducing excessive nerve signals reaching the heart. Procedures such as stellate ganglion nerve blocks temporarily interrupt nerve activity, while denervation involves disrupting certain nerve pathways.

Understanding how the left and right nerve clusters differ could eventually help physicians determine which side should be targeted for the greatest benefit.

Dr. Coppi explained: "Irregular heart rhythms, known as arrhythmias, stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome, and certain types of chest pain are often treated by dialing down overactive stellate ganglia -- the paired small nerve hubs in the lower neck/upper chest area that send 'go faster' signals to the heart.

"By mapping how exercise changes these ganglia on each side, the study offers clues that could one day fine-tune procedures like nerve blocks or denervation to the side most likely to help. The findings are early-stage and in rats, so clinical studies would need to follow."

What's Next for Exercise and Heart Research?

Although the structural changes were substantial, scientists still need to establish exactly how they affect heart function.

The research team plans to investigate whether the differences between the left and right nerve clusters influence how the heart behaves during rest and physical activity. They also intend to look for similar patterns in other animal models and eventually in humans.

For human studies, the researchers hope to use noninvasive markers, which could provide information about nerve activity without requiring surgery or tissue removal.

If the same left-right differences are found in people, the discovery could help guide more personalized treatments for arrhythmias, difficult-to-treat angina, and stress-induced 'broken-heart' syndrome.

Dr. Coppi added: "Understanding these left-right differences could help us personalize treatments for heart rhythm disorders and angina. Our next step is to test how these structural changes map onto function and whether similar patterns appear in larger animals and humans."

#738. Evacuation from Oleshky: How are preparations going?

A lawyer with the Save Ukraine Foundation, Myroslava Kharchenko, told DW about what has been happening in Russian-occupied Oleshky since a temporary ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump took effect.

Since a ceasefire took effect in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region on October 27, preparations have been underway to evacuate residents trapped there.

Following Russia's occupation of the town in 2022 and the flooding caused by the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023, residents were cut off from the outside world. All access routes to Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River, had been mined. Former Oleshky residents who managed to escape and talked to DW described hunger, no access to medicine, and no electricity or water. About 2,000 people are still living in the town.

According to the Save Ukraine Foundation, it has rescued at least 300 civilians from Oleshky over the past six months. DW spoke with lawyer Myroslava Kharchenko, who works for the organization, about preparations for the upcoming evacuation.

DW: A ceasefire is already in effect in Oleshky. Do you know whether any evacuation efforts have begun?

Myroslava Kharchenko: No, we do not have that information yet. What we do know is that the ceasefire came into effect on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time, which is 4 a.m. in Russia. Mine-clearing operations on the road began at around 8 a.m. What is happening inside Oleshky itself, however, is entirely within the military's remit. Everyone involved in this operation has been asked to maintain strict confidentiality. Any careless remark or action could jeopardize the entire evacuation effort.

What I can see is that information is being actively collected through closed internal local chat groups. Registration lists and application forms are being shared, and people are filling them out themselves. Organizers are contacting those who previously requested evacuation to verify details such as their date of birth and current place of residence. They are also asking people to provide contact information for neighbors or relatives who may be nearby or in the same building, because communications are extremely unreliable.

The organizers are also collecting information about the health conditions of those planning to leave. Among them are people who are ill, have limited mobility, or are recovering from recent injuries, including blast and mine-related wounds. We therefore expect those organizing the evacuation to ensure that medical assistance is available for those who need it.

How exactly is the evacuation expected to take place? Will people be evacuated through Russian-controlled territory or via the Dnipro River? Have any routes already been agreed upon?

As far as we know, a river route would be extremely dangerous. We have not heard any confirmation that such an option has been approved. It therefore appears likely that the evacuation route will pass through the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and possibly through Russia before people are able to reach Ukraine. For security reasons, however, none of these details are being made public.

What do you know about the number of people expected to be evacuated?

We are actually very pleased that the evacuation is not expected to take place in a single day. That is important because we hope that those who manage to leave safely during the first stage will serve as an example for others.

People still trapped in Oleshky are extremely afraid. There have already been numerous provocations, and this is not the first attempt to establish such a route or humanitarian corridor.

As a result, there is a great deal of suspicion. Those concerns are based largely on uncertainty, and some people may choose not to leave during the initial phase of the evacuation. Overall, however, we estimate that around 500 people may eventually be evacuated.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How would you assess the role of Melania Trump in making this evacuation possible?

We are immensely grateful to Melania Trump for drawing attention to the humanitarian catastrophe currently unfolding in Oleshky. What is taking place there is in fact genocide committed by the Russian Federation.

We are thankful for her efforts and hope they will help make this evacuation possible. We will be even more grateful once most people are safely removed from the combat zone and arrive in Ukrainian government-controlled territory.

When could the physical evacuation of civilians begin?

I can't say how long it will take. What seems clear, however, is that time will be needed to clear mines from the roads leading into the city. We also understand that many streets inside Oleshky are mined, so additional work will be required to make routes within the city safe.

There is a hospital from which people need to be evacuated. Nearby is a morgue where bodies also need to be recovered.

I do not know whether that will be included as part of this humanitarian corridor, but it is undoubtedly important. The bodies need to be identified and the causes of death established. That process will also take time, regardless of how quickly the military is able to work.

It is difficult to make any predictions because, as you can see, everything is being conducted under strict secrecy. Statements from both the Russian and Ukrainian sides have been extremely cautious, and that is clearly justified under the circumstances.

#736. Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue

Scientists at the University of Bonn have discovered that spiders experience distinct stages of sleep, including a REM-like state that shares surprising similarities with human sleep. During this stage, the spiders move their eyes and twitch their muscles, behaviors also associated with REM (rapid eye movement) sleep in humans and other vertebrates.

The findings provide the first comprehensive experimental confirmation that spiders experience genuine, regulated sleep rather than simply remaining inactive. They also raise intriguing questions about how sleep evolved and whether animals with very different nervous systems might share some of its fundamental features.

Researchers at the University of Bonn's Institute of Organismic Biology made the discovery while studying the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a small but remarkably sophisticated predator.

A Tiny Spider With Remarkable Hunting Skills

The Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata is only about the size of a one-euro coin when fully grown, but its hunting abilities make it particularly interesting to scientists.

Unlike many spiders that primarily capture insects, members of the genus Portia specialize in hunting other spiders. They use a variety of sophisticated strategies to catch their prey, including imitating the vibrations made by struggling insects trapped in spiderwebs.

These deceptive signals can lure web-building spiders toward what appears to be an easy meal, only for them to encounter the hunting Portia instead.

Such complex behaviors suggest that these spiders have unusual learning abilities, making them valuable subjects for investigating the relationship between sleep, nervous system function, and cognition.

Scientists Discover Two Distinct Stages of Spider Sleep

Although sleep has been extensively studied in humans and other vertebrates, scientists still know relatively little about how it works in animals with very different nervous systems.

To investigate whether spiders experience genuine sleep and whether that sleep includes different stages, the researchers closely monitored Portia fimbriata over several days and nights.

They discovered that the spiders exhibit two clearly distinguishable sleep stages. One of these resembles REM sleep, the phase in humans associated with rapid eye movements, muscle activity, and vivid dreaming.

During this REM-like stage, the spiders displayed characteristic eye movements and muscle twitches. These observations suggest that some features of sleep previously studied mainly in vertebrates may also occur in spiders.

The researchers emphasize that identifying REM-like movements does not establish whether spiders dream. However, the discovery provides important evidence that sleep in these animals is more complex than previously understood.

How Researchers Confirmed That Spiders Really Sleep

To study the spiders' sleeping behavior, the team placed individual Portia fimbriata spiders in plastic dishes measuring 12 centimeters in diameter. They monitored the animals under different lighting conditions to examine their daily activity and rest cycles.

Infrared cameras allowed the researchers to observe the spiders throughout the night without relying on visible light. Detailed recordings captured their sleeping positions, periods of quiet rest, and episodes of REM-like movement.

The team also conducted experiments to determine whether the spiders were genuinely asleep rather than simply sitting motionless.

Using sound stimuli, the researchers measured how quickly the spiders responded to disturbances. These tests helped distinguish sleep from ordinary inactivity.

Another important part of the investigation involved sleep deprivation. The researchers examined whether the spiders displayed "sleep rebound," meaning they compensated for interrupted sleep by increasing their subsequent sleep.

Together, the behavioral observations and experimental tests provided strong evidence that Portia fimbriata experiences regulated sleep with distinct stages.

Studying Spider Sleep Presented Unusual Challenges

Determining whether a spider is truly asleep is considerably more complicated than observing a sleeping human.

Because spiders sense their surroundings differently from people, the researchers first had to identify a sound stimulus that would produce a consistent response during their experiments.

They also needed to avoid assuming that the observed eye movements and muscle twitches necessarily represented the same processes seen during human REM sleep.

One major limitation was that the researchers could not measure the spiders' brain activity. Instead, they relied entirely on carefully documented behavior to identify different sleep states.

This required extensive high-resolution video recordings collected over many days and nights, producing enormous amounts of data for analysis.

Despite these obstacles, the combination of behavioral monitoring, response testing, and sleep disruption experiments allowed the researchers to build a detailed picture of how these spiders sleep.

What Spider Sleep Could Reveal About Evolution

The discovery has implications that extend well beyond spiders.

Most scientific knowledge about sleep comes from studying vertebrates, particularly mammals and birds. Finding comparable sleep features in animals with radically different nervous systems could help researchers understand when and why different types of sleep evolved.

The results also open new opportunities in behavioral science, neuroscience, and chronobiology, the study of biological rhythms.

By investigating sleep in a wider variety of animals, scientists hope to identify features that are shared across species and uncover the fundamental biological functions that sleep may have served early in evolutionary history.

The researchers argue that future investigations should move beyond traditionally studied animals and include species with unusual adaptations or much simpler nervous systems.

Such comparisons could reveal whether certain sleep mechanisms are widespread throughout the animal kingdom or developed independently in different evolutionary lineages.

Even after decades of intensive research, many basic questions about sleep remain unanswered, including important mysteries surrounding human sleep.

Could Spiders Dream? Scientists Have More Questions

The University of Bonn team is now expanding its research to investigate how sleep, particularly REM-like sleep, varies across different spider species.

Scientists are also comparing spiders sleeping in natural environments with those observed in laboratories to determine how surroundings influence their behavior.

Another major goal is to investigate the relationship between sleep and cognitive abilities. Researchers want to understand what happens inside the brains of spiders and insects during sleep, and whether different sleep stages contribute to learning and other mental processes.

Environmental changes are also becoming an important focus. The team plans to examine how climate change and human activities, especially artificial light at night (ALAN), may interfere with the sleep patterns of spiders and other arthropods.

For now, the findings establish that even a tiny jumping spider can experience a surprisingly complex form of sleep. Whether spiders actually dream remains unknown, but their nighttime behavior is offering scientists new clues about one of biology's most enduring mysteries.

#734. Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe

Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever developed, offering a remarkable new way to explore how the cosmos evolved after the Big Bang. Known as "Lumina," the simulation was built by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian to help astronomers interpret observations from powerful instruments such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope.

The research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, reconstructs the universe's first 2 billion years by modeling the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation. By comparing Lumina's predictions with observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes, scientists can evaluate how well existing theories explain cosmic evolution and identify discoveries that might challenge their understanding of the universe's fundamental laws.

Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing explanations for the formation of stars, galaxies, and other cosmic structures. Modern supercomputers now make it possible to turn these ideas into detailed simulations that predict how the universe should behave. When telescope observations agree with those predictions, they strengthen confidence in current theories. Unexpected differences, however, may point toward physical processes that scientists have yet to fully understand.

"With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics," said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. "To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video."

Recreating the Universe's First 2 Billion Years

Lumina is the largest cosmological radiation hydrodynamics simulation ever produced. In simple terms, it uses powerful computers to calculate how gas, dark matter, and light influenced one another as the young universe developed. By following these interactions across the first 2 billion years after the Big Bang, researchers can examine how the earliest galaxies formed and how their activity changed the enormous clouds of gas surrounding them.

The simulation models a volume of space more than 100 times larger than those covered by earlier comparable projects. Its virtual universe spans a cube approximately 1.5 billion light-years on each side, providing a view of cosmic evolution on a scale comparable to the vast regions that today's most advanced telescopes can study.

Another major advance is Lumina's treatment of helium reionization, a process in which radiation strips electrons from helium atoms. For the first time, a simulation of this kind follows that transformation as it unfolds while simultaneously accounting for how it affects the surrounding universe. This allows scientists to study the relationship between evolving galaxies, radiation, and the gas that fills the space between them.

"We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina," said Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper. "For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation."

A Massive Supercomputer Powers the Virtual Cosmos

Recreating such an enormous portion of cosmic history demanded extraordinary computing resources. The team used more than 15,000 graphics processing units on Frontier, one of the world's fastest supercomputers, housed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

That processing power enabled the researchers to simulate an exceptionally large region of the early universe without sacrificing the fine detail needed to investigate individual galaxies and other important structures. As a result, Lumina can capture the broader evolution of the cosmos while also tracking processes involved in the formation of stars, galaxies, and black holes.

Testing the Mysteries of the Early Universe

Beyond recreating cosmic history, Lumina provides a powerful new framework for investigating how the universe developed. Researchers plan to use it to explore the movement of gas between galaxies, the influence of radiation left over from the Big Bang, and the emergence of regions where stars formed at especially high rates.

By placing these predictions alongside observations from the James Webb Space Telescope, the Nancy Roman Space Telescope, and other instruments, scientists hope to build a more complete picture of the universe's earliest chapters. Any unexpected differences between the simulated cosmos and the real one could provide valuable clues, potentially revealing where current theories need to be refined or reconsidered.

#733. Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany's health scare highlights the need for better support for elite coaches

Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.

Vincent Kompany has just returned home from hospital. The Bayern Munich head coach admitted that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

Bayern Munich's sporting director Max Eberl, who left Gladbach in 2022 due to his own health concerns, told German public broadcaster ARD that the 40-year-old Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation, which if untreated can become meningitis.

"They found out what it is. It is a meningeal irritation that brought on the incident last Friday," said Eberl, referring to when Kompany collapsed during training and required an emergency doctor.

"Honestly, he is doing as well as can be expected. He has been discharged from hospital today, which is the biggest and best news for all of us."

The news has been met by great concern from the German football community. Bayern fans held a banner showing their support, many German media outlets wrote opinion articles softly reminding that coaches are humans too and they too need support. Even the wider coaching community has started to ask questions.

"It’s something you take to heart and think about," Freiburg head coach Julian Schuster said after his team lost to Bayern recently.

"We coaches aren’t always very good at taking care of ourselves in those situations."

Eberl, though, shut down the suggestion that this was related to pressure or stress.

"It's an illness. Any one of us can get it. It has nothing to do with the pressure we face in the Bundesliga," Eberl said.

Nevertheless, with Kompany admitting he hadn't listened to his body and his assistant coach Aaron Danks saying that "getting Vince to rest is a challenge", it is clear that the Belgian had been working very hard of late.

Kompany, whose father became the first Black mayor in Belgium after moving there from the DR Congo, has faced an enormous amount of adversity in his life. At just 14, his parents divorced and he told The Guardian in a 2019 interview: "I need to be fed stuff constantly, otherwise I don’t know how to function. I can't remember a lazy Sunday."

The Belgian's own history, both in his childhood and as former professional player, also plays a role in understanding the challenges coaches face in elite sport.

"I think we (coaches) have a really poor measure of ourselves within this example of like, wasn't listening to my body. I think a lot of coaches are really poor at that,"  coaching mentor Cody Royle, who has worked with teams in the NBA and the Premier League, told DW.

"And so part of my role is to enhance their attunement to that, to ask questions to that effect, to try to perhaps even impart some things that I've learned along the way or heard from others or other coaches that are going through similar things so that you can actually start to put words to what that feeling might have been or where you maybe touched burnout but it didn't quite get there and you're able to rescue something and start to really develop skill within it," he said.

"I think with Vincent's example we also need to account for the fact that this is a young man still finding his way in coaching and so he's still understanding what those triggers are within his body and what they're really telling him Maybe he had physical things that he could read when he was playing. These are more mental triggers, and he's still learning that and that's part of what he needs to do. But there should be people around that help."

It begs the question, in 2026, at a time when awareness around mental and physical health is greater than ever, particularly in elite sport, how is this still possible?

"I suspect that many head coaches aren't able to let go or delegate," Frank Wormuth, an educator for the German Football Association (DFB), told DW.

"They want to control everything because they don't feel secure when the team loses," continued Wormuth, adding that that's why coaches often bring close friends into their staff.

"You'd think professional coaches wouldn't have to worry, since they've earned enough money, but that’s not a good coach's priority—success is far more important."

A former coach, Wormuth admits that he had moments in his career when he had lost sight of how much of a role football was playing in his life.

"I never felt like I was doing too much until my kids pointed out to me—when I was at home—that I wasn't the coach anymore, but should be fulfilling the role of a father," Wormuth said.

"That's when I realized that I was truly operating 24/7 as a coach in my head, even when I was at home."

Royle believes coaches need to learn more about how to manage themselves.

"I kind of throw my hands up a little bit at the fact that we aren't further along," Royle said.

"We're not even trying to educate this in to our young coaches as they come through. The education system probably facilitates this as much as the organizations that are individually responsible."

Clearly, if not well managed, extremely demanding elite-sports environments with high expectations on individuals makes for a dangerous combination. Both Wormuth and Royle advocate for the concept of a second set of eyes.

"Maybe it is that there's a mechanism now for coaches to really investigate," Royle said.

Having someone who sits outside the organization and doesn't belong to the politics to be able to —whether it's on the phone or come in for a visit — just say, 'You need to go home because this isn't going well.'"

"This is a game where Jock Stein literally dropped dead on the sideline, right? There shouldn't need to be any more conversation beyond that... and it was workaholism and stress that caused it," added Royle.

"So I don't know what else it's going to take, but I just don't think the game really cares enough to change anything about it. The show must go on, right?"

Even as it does when Bayern Munich play Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga's most marketed game this weekend, Kompany's absence will serve as a reminder that while much of the focus of modern sport is on the players, there is an equal level of support required for those on the sidelines.

#731. James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”

Astronomers have discovered surprising evidence that a scorching planet covered in molten rock may be protected by a reflective layer of clouds that acts like a giant sunscreen. Scientists previously believed that the planet's extreme conditions would make it nearly impossible for an atmosphere to survive, but new observations suggest otherwise.

An international team of researchers, including Dr. Anjali Piette, an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham, reported the findings in The Astronomical Journal. Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the scientists monitored a rocky exoplanet called TOI-561 b, located approximately 280 light-years from Earth. Over 37 hours, they observed nearly four complete orbits around its host star.

The observations indicate that TOI-561 b may be surrounded by a substantial atmosphere, although its conditions would be far too hostile for life as we know it. This atmosphere appears to help the planet reflect much of the radiation coming from its star. One possible explanation is a layer of highly reflective silicate clouds that prevents the surface from reaching the extreme temperatures expected on an exposed rocky planet. The atmosphere also appears to move heat from the permanently illuminated dayside toward the nightside, further reducing temperatures on the star-facing side.

A Lava Planet With an Atmosphere That Should Have Disappeared

Scientists still do not know exactly which gases make up the atmosphere of TOI-561 b. One possibility is a thick layer of carbon dioxide, resembling the atmosphere of Venus but under much hotter conditions. Another is an atmosphere dominated by sulfur dioxide, a gas released by volcanic activity on Jupiter's moon Io.

Dr. Anjali Piette, Assistant Professor in Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, said: "Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.

"Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today. This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface, acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere."

James Webb Reveals Why the Planet Is So Reflective

Earlier measurements revealed something puzzling about TOI-561 b. Its dayside was significantly cooler than researchers predicted for a dark, rocky planet orbiting so close to its star. That unexpected temperature suggested that much of the incoming energy was either being transferred to the nightside or reflected back into space before it could heat the surface.

To investigate, the team observed the planet throughout its orbit, allowing them to examine its nightside for the first time. Because the same side of TOI-561 b always faces its star, the nightside receives no direct starlight. However, the measurements showed that this darker hemisphere was not warm enough to explain all the missing heat.

The findings instead indicate that TOI-561 b reflects approximately 75% of the starlight reaching it, a remarkably high proportion comparable to Venus.

To determine what could produce such strong reflectivity, the researchers compared the telescope measurements with computer models of the planet's climate. Their simulations suggest that clouds containing silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide (SiO2) and magnesium silicate (MgSiO3), may form over the dayside. If present, these clouds could reflect incoming radiation before it reaches the surface, functioning as a natural sunscreen.

Professor Lisa Dang, who led the project at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, said: "We measured how the planet's brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit. This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere."

Could a Global Ocean of Lava Keep the Atmosphere Alive?

The new findings strengthen earlier evidence gathered by Professor Lisa Dang, Dr. Anjali Piette, and their collaborators that TOI-561 b has a thick atmosphere that may be continually replenished by gases escaping from its molten interior.

That possibility could help explain how the planet has maintained an atmosphere despite enduring intense radiation from its star for billions of years. Rather than simply losing its gases to space, the planet's vast reservoir of molten rock may be constantly releasing new material into the atmosphere.

Researchers now hope to determine whether TOI-561 b is more like an extremely hot Venus or a much more intense version of the volcanic moon Io. Additional observations with JWST at longer wavelengths could reveal important details about the atmosphere's chemical composition and help resolve the mystery of its long-term survival.

Professor Dang added: "The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b's atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of lo. Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years."

Materials provided by University of Birmingham. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#729. Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body

Medications are designed to treat diseases and relieve symptoms, but some can also produce unintended effects that put patients at risk. While side effects are common with many treatments, researchers have identified a particularly concerning possibility involving drugs used to control inflammation.

Scientists at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) have discovered that a widely used class of anti-inflammatory medications may make it easier for certain viruses to infect cells and spread throughout the body.

"We have found a surprising and potentially serious side effect of a class of anti-inflammatory drugs. They can help viruses spread more easily in the body," says Denis Kainov, a professor at the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

Common Anti-Inflammatory Drugs May Help Viruses Spread

The medications at the center of the findings belong to a class called Janus kinase inhibitors, or JAKs. These drugs are widely prescribed to control inflammation, but their effects on the immune system may also leave the body more vulnerable to viral infections.

"Among the viruses that more easily affect the body with the help of these drugs are Rift Valley fever virus, influenza A, adenovirus and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19," Kainov says.

These viruses can cause significant illness, making any treatment that potentially increases their ability to spread a serious concern.

Why Arthritis Drugs Can Weaken Antiviral Defenses

In a new study published in NAR Molecular Medicine, Kainov and his colleagues investigated how JAK inhibitors influence the body's ability to defend itself against viruses.

"JAK inhibitors are often prescribed for autoimmune diseases and inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis," says Erlend Ravlo, a PhD research fellow at NTNU and first author of the article.

Although these medications can be highly effective at reducing inflammation, their benefits come with an important trade-off. By suppressing certain immune responses, they can also interfere with the mechanisms that normally protect the body from viral infections.

"In particular, the drugs suppress an important immune signalling pathway that helps protect healthy cells from viral attacks," Ravlo said.

This pathway plays a central role in coordinating the body's response when viruses attempt to infect healthy tissue.

Scientists Discover How JAK Inhibitors Disrupt Immune Protection

The research team found that JAK inhibitors, including the medication baricitinib, can reduce the activity of genes involved in fighting viral infections.

"These genes play a crucial role in the body's response to viral infections," said Aleksandr Ianevski, an NTNU researcher and coauthor of the new paper.

When JAK inhibitors interfere with this immune signaling system, they weaken an important layer of antiviral protection. Without the usual defensive response, viruses may find it easier to establish an infection and spread between cells.

To investigate these effects, the scientists combined advanced virology methods with gene expression analysis and organoid technology. Their experiments included cells from the lungs, eyes and brain, along with miniature organ models grown in the laboratory.

These approaches allowed the team to examine how the drugs affect antiviral defenses across different types of human tissue.

"Although JAK inhibitors are effective in the treatment of inflammation, this shows that they can pose a hidden risk for patients who have latent or active viral infections," says Ravlo.

What the Findings Mean for Patients and Future Treatments

The results highlight the importance of carefully considering the risks associated with JAK inhibitors, particularly when patients may already have a viral infection or when outbreaks are occurring.

Researchers suggest that healthcare professionals should exercise caution when prescribing these medications during periods of increased viral transmission.

However, the same immune-suppressing properties that create potential risks for patients could also offer advantages in certain research settings. Under controlled laboratory conditions, these effects may help scientists develop vaccines or evaluate potential antiviral medications.

The researchers hope their findings will encourage greater awareness of how JAK inhibitors influence the immune system and support further investigations into their safest and most effective uses.

"We recommend further studies to better understand how the drugs can be used optimally, especially during virus outbreaks or pandemics," says Ianevski.

Professor Magnar Bjørås of the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine provided significant scientific expertise and secured most of the funding for the research. Additional financial support came from the Central Norway Regional Health Authority, the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority, the Research Council of Norway and the Swedish Research Council.

#728. ‘Something To Lose’: Behind Stella Lefty’s Winning Duet With Vincent Mason: ‘I’m So Grateful That We’re Doing This Together’

Billboard's Makin' Tracks highlights the recording and writing behind "Something to Lose."

It was intended, according to Stella Lefty’s lyrics, as a little “something to do.”

But a meet-up with fellow country artist Vincent Mason turned into something much greater. Eight months later, they’re fully public about a relationship that developed from that original meeting, and her something to do is now “Something to Lose” on two fronts — it’s a way to describe the value they put on their romantic connection, but it’s also the title of their first duet.

“Once we started dating,” she says, “it was just this inevitable thing, like, ‘There’s this song that’s so personal about our relationship and the way that things started and the way that I feel about you.’ It just made so much sense.” Related Justin Timberlake to Release 4-Part Docuseries That Includes Janet Jackson as a Guest Bruce Springsteen Backs Michigan's Dr. Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate Amid Haley Stevens Reversal: 'He's a Fighter' Tate McRae's 'Housewife' Scores Second Week at No. 1 on Billboard Global Charts Explore Stella Lefty See latest videos, charts and news

It was not an ideal time, career-wise, to start a new relationship. Mason had been hitting it hard as a new artist for several years, taking every promotional opportunity available and finally on his way to his first top 20 on Billboard’s Country Airplay with “Wish You Well.” Lefty’s “Thinking ‘Bout You” was bringing her first real taste of commercial significance, leading to her February 2026 signing with Atlantic/Outpost, and the schedule she anticipated didn’t have room for someone new.

“I felt like I was [just being] born into this,” she says, “like, entering for the first time, and so I felt like I was in a weird place. I was like, ‘Oh, my god, I need to accept being alone because I’m experiencing all these things for the first time, and I need to figure this out.’”

Mason, after seeing her on TikTok, sent her a direct message. She responded, and they met up in early 2026 at Schulman’s, a neighborhood bar in East Nashville. Just to be safe, she brought along a few industry friends: songwriters Grace Enger (“Boston”) and Jacob “JKash” Hindlin (“Last Night,” “After All the Bars are Closed”) and writer-producer Joe Reeves (Thomas Rhett, Lil Durk).

“Grace got a burger inside while [Lefty] was talking to Vincent outside,” Reeves recalls. “We were drinking chartreuse, and it was quite a funny night.”

Monumental, as well, since the two singers hit it off immediately. Both had to leave town, but when their schedules lined up again, they saw each other for several days. Enger and Lefty were sharing quarters, so Enger witnessed the start of the relationship. The two women ended up writing with Jon Decious (“4x4xU,” “Phone, Keys, Wallet”) and Luke Dick (“Choosin’ Texas,” “Don’t Come Lookin’”) in Nashville on Feb. 18, spending six hours on another song, though Lefty was somewhat distracted.

“While we were writing this other song, I kept singing something about ‘wild horses,’” Lefty notes, “and so when we finished the first song, I was like, ‘Can we just try something for five seconds? I have this idea, but I don’t know what it is.’ Grace started playing chords on the guitar, and we literally wrote the song in 20 minutes or something.”

Her initial idea turned into the first line of the chorus, “I was a wild horse built for runnin’,” about a woman who is unexpectedly considering a romantic commitment. Monogamy, of course, implies sacrificing certain freedoms.

“I thought about the [Kris] Kristofferson song, ‘Bobby McGee,’ you know, ‘Freedom’s just another word for nothin’ left to lose,’” Decious says. “I was like, ‘What’s the opposite of that?’ So, ‘Something to Lose,’ and then we kept throwing around lines.”

They opened the song with a nod to her independent streak, then alluded to the Schulman’s introduction — “2:00 a.m. in a Southern state” — and edged into the chorus. Enger, of course, knew firsthand who they were writing about. The men hadn’t a clue.

“She kept giggling, as if there was some new love in her life,” Decious says. “It would come to different lines — I think ‘blue eyes comin’,’ I think maybe it was ‘green’ initially — and she’s like, ‘No, he’s got blue eyes.’ We were picking up on the idea that maybe there was somebody new in her life, but she didn’t mention it, and she certainly never said, ‘Oh, this is about Vincent Mason’.”

Songs about new love usually lean upbeat and optimistic, but “Something to Lose” approaches the topic with caution and fragility. “I got good at bein’ lonely ‘til you showed me I was better with you,” she sings, but the plaintive sonics convey reservation: the pangs of excitement might only be temporary.

“I think it’s an overall reflection of where he was at,” she says, “and what I was sensing from him, and my fear of, you know, there’s something real here, but ‘What if you don’t want that?’”

The writers made a quick guitar/vocal demo on a cellphone, each receiving a copy by 4 p.m. At 7:01 p.m., Decious reconnected with the group: “Y’all, just listening back, and this song is killer.” At some point, Lefty and Enger played the song for Mason. Lefty later sent him the demo. And she told Mason it was about him. “That was a good bit of information to find out,” he says. “And then she was like, ‘You got to sing it with me.’”

He said yes, but not just because she was asking. “I do love Stella,” he says, “but I would not have got on there if it was a bad song.”

Reeves built the track in his home studio in Los Angeles’ Echo Park, playing all of the stringed instruments — guitars, mandolin, banjo and bass — intentionally keeping it sparse so their voices would stand out. The moments when he did step forward were significant to the flow of the track, such as a mid-chorus turn-around that layers acoustic guitar and a Telecaster with old-school tremolo.

The key was initially difficult for Vincent, but they re-pitched it in time for an April 10 vocal session. Reeves and vocal producer Brett Truitt (Waylon Wyatt, Maddox Batson) were present as the couple recorded their vocals together, holding hands in the closet-sized vocal booth at Truitt’s Nashville studio. “We’re like little kids,” Lefty says.

It was, Mason adds, “maybe a little awkward, maybe a little scary,” since they were singing together for the first time. A day later, Evan Hutchings overdubbed drums on the track. Reeves also enlisted London-based steel guitarist Joe Harvey-Whyte, who contributed a Poco/Flying Burrito Brothers feel.

“I don’t think what he draws from intuitively is Nashville voicings, but there is a riff he plays halfway through Vincent’s verse that, in my opinion, makes the song complete,” Reeves says. “I know both Vincent and Stella are very happy with that, because whenever we do it live, they’re like, ‘We need that riff. Someone needs to play that.’”

“Something to Lose” went out to the world in May, and the couple found several opportunities to play it live. As Lefty’s “Boston” ran its course, Atlantic/Outpost teed up “Something to Lose” for country radio, releasing it via PlayMPE on Sept. 22.

“People really took to it on TikTok in a way that it just kind of raised its hand,” Mason says.

It’s at No. 28 on Billboard’s Country Airplay chart dated Nov. 7, and No. 13 on the parallel Hot Country Songs. Their relationship has developed further in the eight months since she wrote “Something to Lose,” and they’re both confident they’ll keep growing together, with “Something” reminding them of their start as a couple.

“It’s been such a crazy year for me personally, and also for Vincent personally,” she says. “He’s helped me get through so much of the things that I’ve been dealing with, and I’m so grateful that we’re doing this together.

#727. The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs may have helped ants conquer the world

Around 66 million years ago, an asteroid struck Earth and brought the age of the dinosaurs to an end. The mass extinction that followed created opportunities for countless other animals to evolve and spread. Ants were among the groups that eventually became remarkably successful, and scientists have now identified a surprising genetic factor that may have helped fuel their rise.

Today, ants are the largest family of social insects, with more than 15,000 species found around the world. New research published in Science Advances suggests that their extraordinary evolutionary success was partly driven by mobile segments of DNA known as transposable elements, or "jumping genes."

The international study was led by Dr. Lukas Schrader of the Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity (IEB) at the University of Münster (Germany).

Jumping genes are pieces of DNA that can move to different locations within a genome and produce additional copies of themselves. Scientists once viewed them primarily as "genomic parasites" because, much like viruses, they can multiply without providing any clear benefit to their host. In some cases, their activity can even contribute to disease.

More recently, however, researchers have begun recognizing that these mobile genetic elements can also create opportunities for evolutionary change. The new findings suggest they played an important role in the remarkable diversification of ants.

When the scientists compared different groups of ants, they discovered that lineages containing the greatest numbers of jumping genes also tended to have the most species today.

Even more revealing was the timing of these genetic changes. The researchers found that several major ant lineages experienced separate surges in jumping gene activity during the early Paleogene (about 66 million years ago). These bursts occurred shortly before the groups began expanding into the thousands of species that exist today.

"The asteroid impact had dramatic consequences for the environment. We have now found the genomic mechanism that connects these ecological upheavals to the subsequent rapid diversification of the ants: transposable elements," explains Lukas Schrader.

Ants are not the only animals showing this evolutionary pattern. Previous studies have also identified periods of increased jumping gene activity associated with the emergence of new species in other groups, including primates and bats.

The researchers also discovered a connection between jumping genes and the expansion of gene families that allow ants to communicate through chemical signals.

Of particular importance were genes responsible for odorant receptors, which enable ants to detect and respond to smells. These receptors are essential to nearly every aspect of ant social behavior. Ants depend heavily on chemical cues to find their way through the environment, identify members of their own colonies, and coordinate activities with other ants.

The findings suggest that jumping genes may have contributed to the expansion of these sensory systems, potentially improving the ability of ants to detect and interpret the chemical messages that make their complex societies possible.

Tracing 100 Million Years of Ant Evolution

To investigate how jumping genes influenced ant evolution, the international research team examined and compared the genomes of 163 ant species. These represented twelve of the 16 ant subfamilies that survive today, providing a broad picture of the genetic diversity found across modern ants.

Using these genomic comparisons, the scientists reconstructed how transposable elements evolved and changed in activity over the past 100 million years.

Their results reveal a striking connection between ancient bursts of jumping gene activity and the later diversification of ants, suggesting that DNA sequences once dismissed as genetic parasites may have helped one of Earth's most successful insect groups flourish.

#726. Universities must measure learning, both with and without AI assistance

To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Marc Schmitt argues that the danger of artificial intelligence lies in passive use, and that universities should teach students to argue with AI models and assess how well they do so (see M. Schmitt Nature 657, 575; 2026). One measurement is missing. Assessing how a student spars while the model is present captures performance with the partner in the ring, not what the student can do once the partner leaves. The two can diverge: in a randomized trial involving secondary-school mathematics students, unrestricted chatbot access raised practice scores, but lowered performance on a subsequent exam taken without it (H. Bastani et al. Proc. Natl Acad. Sci. USA 122, e2422633122; 2025). An evaluation that stopped at the assisted session would have called that tutor a success.

Grande also offered another look at her new bob, which she first debuted in late October. One image shows a side view of the cut, featuring a playful swoop that falls just above her shoulders, while another captures a sideways selfie showcasing the sleek style, accessorized with a white ribbon choker.

The singer also shared a behind-the-scenes glimpse of hairstylist Brandon Pietsch appearing to wash her hair.

“The bob is everything mommy,” actress Rachel Zegler wrote in the comments. The singer’s brother Frankie Grande added, “Cute happy girlie pop! I love you so!”

Grande also shared a photo of herself holding Enthousiasmos, a culture magazine whose third issue features her Wicked co-star Jeff Goldblum. The pair became friends while filming the movies, and later collaborated on Goldblum’s 2025 album, Still Blooming.

#724. Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction

Scientists at the University of St Andrews have identified a previously unknown process that may help explain how Earth entered past ice ages. Their findings reveal a surprising connection between ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere and ocean changes near Antarctica, suggesting that cooling in one part of the world could trigger a chain reaction affecting the entire planet.

The study, published in the Journal of Climate, offers a possible explanation for how growing northern ice sheets influenced ocean circulation and sea ice in the Southern Hemisphere. These southern changes are known to help reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2), an important factor in the development of ice ages. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain how processes occurring at opposite ends of the planet could be so closely connected.

One of the main forces behind Earth's past ice ages was a reduction in atmospheric CO2 as more carbon became stored in the oceans. Much of this process was controlled by changes in the Southern Ocean surrounding Antarctica. However, a major question remained unanswered: How could expanding ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere, initially driven by natural variations in Earth's orbit, cause the distant Southern Ocean to absorb more CO2?

How Northern Ice Sheets Could Trigger Changes Near Antarctica

The researchers propose that the answer lies in the movement of ocean water between the hemispheres. As large ice sheets spread across northern regions, they cool nearby waters in the North Atlantic. Over time, these colder waters circulate southward, eventually reaching the Southern Ocean.

If the cooling is sufficiently strong, it could alter ocean circulation around Antarctica in ways that allow more CO2 to be stored beneath the ocean's surface. As atmospheric CO2 declines, the planet cools further, potentially helping intensify an ice age.

To investigate this possibility, the team used computer simulations of ocean circulation. Rather than lowering temperatures across the entire planet, they cooled only the northernmost latitudes (mimicking the effect of a large ice sheet) and examined how the Southern Ocean responded.

The results were striking. Cooling the far northern regions alone produced 74% as much CO2 drawdown as a separate simulation in which the entire planet was cooled. This suggests that temperature changes in the Northern Hemisphere could have a powerful influence on the Southern Ocean and its ability to store carbon.

A Missing Link in Earth's Ice Age Mystery

The simulations provide strong support for the proposed connection between expanding northern ice sheets and changes in the Southern Ocean. They suggest that colder water originating in the North Atlantic could eventually influence circulation around Antarctica, helping remove CO2 from the atmosphere and contributing to the global cooling associated with past ice ages.

For decades, much of the research into ice age climate changes has concentrated on the Southern Ocean because of its important role in controlling atmospheric carbon dioxide. Only more recently have scientists begun to recognize how changes in distant ocean regions might influence these processes.

Lead author Dr. Madison Shankle, from the University of St Andrews School of Earth and Environmental Science, explained the importance of the findings:

"Essentially, we've produced evidence of a plausible mechanism connecting these two far-flung puzzles pieces - Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and Southern Hemisphere ocean circulation changes leading to CO2 drawdown - which has been a tricky thing to explain in our theory of Earth's past ice ages. Our study takes the step of actually demonstrating them working in model simulations, which is a big step forward for this field."

What Ancient Ice Ages Reveal About Today's Climate

Understanding how past ice ages developed offers scientists a valuable way to study Earth's natural carbon cycle. These periods reveal how carbon dioxide moves between the atmosphere and oceans, and how changes in that balance can influence global temperatures.

By identifying another mechanism that may have helped reduce atmospheric CO2 during ancient ice ages, researchers can develop a more complete picture of how Earth's climate system operates.

That knowledge is especially important today, as scientists work to understand how the planet's oceans and other natural systems will respond to the additional carbon dioxide now entering the Earth system.

#723. Michigan ‘Let’s Go Blue’ Composers Settle Lawsuit Over ‘College Football’ Video Game Synch

The now-resolved dispute questioned whether music publishers had the right to license the iconic marching band fight song to Electronic Arts.

The composers of the University of Michigan’s iconic “Let’s Go Blue” marching band fight song have settled legal claims over a synch placement in the College Football video game franchise.

A Monday (Nov. 2) court filing, obtained and first reported by Billboard, says a settlement has been reached resolving “all issues” in the music licensing dispute that began this past March. Deal terms were not disclosed.

The lawsuit stemmed from a license inked by music publishers Theodore Presser and Carl Fischer with Electronic Arts (EA) in 2024 to feature “Let’s Go Blue” in the popular video game College Football, which returned that year from a long hiatus after the NCAA loosened player restrictions on name, image and likeness rights.

Presser and Fischer claimed they’d had continuous rights to administer “Let’s Go Blue” since signing a publishing deal with co-writers Albert Ahronheim and Joe Carl in 1978. But Ahronheim and Carl, who composed the song as students at Michigan, said the composition rights actually reverted back to them years ago — and they weren’t happy to find out the publishers had unilaterally licensed out “Let’s Go Blue” for what they called a “shockingly low” synch fee of just $1,000.

Ahronheim and Carl demanded that EA remove the synch from College Football, and the video game juggernaut complied. This led Presser and Fischer to file a contract interference lawsuit against the composers, who then countersued for copyright infringement. EA itself was not involved in the litigation or accused of any wrongdoing.

Each side sought financial damages from the other, and both wanted a judge to step in and decide the rightful owner of “Let’s Go Blue.” The dispute turned on the termination right, a provision of copyright law that allows authors to claw back intellectual property decades after signing it away. Ahronheim and Carl said they successfully exercised their termination rights in 2013, while the publishers claimed the composers skipped a key technical step in this legal process and therefore did not get the composition reverted.

Reached for comment on the settlement Monday, the publishers’ attorney Brian Caplan told Billboard his clients “are happy that they were able to resolve their differences with Messrs. Ahronheim and Carl, the authors of the iconic song ‘Let’s Go Blue,’ and are looking forward to a mutually beneficial working relationship with the authors.”

Caplan did not say how the settlement resolved the song ownership question or whether “Let’s Go Blue” will now be added back to College Football. Lawyers for Ahronheim and Carl did not return a request for comment. EA declined to comment.

#722. Cinemark Won’t Screen Brad Pitt’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Movie Over Netflix’s Demands, CEO Says

Cinemark boss says agreeing to the streamer's ultra-short two-week release window is "not aligned [with] what's of the greatest interest in our theaters."

Two theater chains are refusing to screen the upcoming sequel to Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood.

Cinemark and Regal have decided against giving any of their Imax screens to The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, which has Brad Pitt reprising his role as a fearless stuntman in a movie written by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher. The decision effectively makes Cliff Booth exclusive to AMC among the major chains.

During Cinemark’s third-quarter earnings call early Tuesday, CEO Sean Gamble explained that the company decided against running the film due to Netflix‘s very short release window — which ends just two weeks before the title shifts to streaming — and not wanting to establish a precedent that could come back to haunt the chain in future negotiations.

“The Cliff Booth situation is an interesting one,” Gamble said. “We book all of our films on a case-by-case situation. In that particular situation, we always look at things through a long-term lens and how certain precedents and things we might do could affect longer-term industry dynamics. In this particular case, we don’t believe the proposed release model is constructive for the broader theatrical ecosystem, and it’s not aligned [with] what’s of the greatest interest in our theaters.” Gamble also added that keeping The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping on its Imax screens during Thanksgiving is a sold play due to the film’s strong advance sales.

Cliff Booth will debut in theaters on Nov. 25, then hit Netflix on Dec. 23.

For Netflix, which has traditionally resisted filmmakers’ efforts to secure theatrical releases for their movies, the film actually represents a first — the first time the streamer has released a movie in Imax. The slot was originally supposed to go to Greta Gerwig’s Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew, but the movie was pushed to February, where it will have a far more generous seven-week theatrical window.

Cinemark Holdings posted higher revenue and earnings compared to a year ago, seeing total revenue rise to $1.05 billion versus $857.5 million in the same period of 2025. Gamble predicted the theatrical window could actually widen despite the rise of streaming.

“We’re going to continue to see [the window] grow, especially since the commitments were a minimum of 45 days and beyond that many of the larger films continue to have windows of 60-plus days,” he said. “As we turn the corner into 2027, we’re going to see that window continue to expand a bit, especially as additional studios join in.”

Etan Vlessing contributed to this report.

#720. Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system

Scientists have uncovered evidence of a previously unknown volcanic system that formed roughly 100 million years ago in what is now northwestern Iran. The discovery reveals a missing chapter in the region's geological history and offers new clues about the powerful tectonic forces that shaped ancient oceans and continents.

Mountain ranges contain valuable records of Earth's distant past, preserving traces of vanished oceans, shifting continents, and the geological processes that transformed the planet over millions of years. However, these records are often difficult to interpret because later tectonic activity, erosion, and layers of buried sediment can conceal evidence of much older events.

An international team led by Istanbul Technical University (ITU) has now identified remnants of an ancient continental magmatic arc that had previously gone unrecognized. Named the Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc, the system formed during the Late Cretaceous period in a region that is now part of the Arabia-Eurasia collision zone.

The research, published in Geoscience Frontiers, indicates that the volcanic system was active approximately 101 to 97 million years ago, when the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean was undergoing major geological changes. Over time, tectonic deformation, erosion, burial beneath sedimentary basins, and a younger episode of volcanic activity during the Eocene obscured much of the evidence of its existence.

Ancient Rocks Reveal a Lost Volcanic System

To reconstruct this overlooked chapter of Earth's history, the researchers examined volcanic and plutonic rocks collected from multiple locations across northwestern Iran. Much of their investigation focused on formations along the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault.

The team used several advanced techniques to determine when the rocks formed and where their original materials came from. These included zircon U-Pb geochronology to establish their ages, Hf isotope analyses to investigate their sources, and whole-rock geochemistry to examine their chemical composition.

Together, the results revealed signatures consistent with continental arc magmatism, a geological process that occurs when one tectonic plate sinks beneath another, generating magma that can rise through the overlying continental crust.

Dr. Ali Mohammadi, the study's corresponding author at Istanbul Technical University, explained: "This study shows that the magmatic history of northwestern Iran is more complex than previously recognized. By integrating geochronological, isotopic, and geochemical evidence, we identified a Late Cretaceous continental arc that was subsequently obscured by later tectonic processes."

The international research effort also involved scientists from the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research and Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences; ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Karadeniz Technical University, Türkiye; and Damghan University, Iran.

A Missing Piece of Iran's Geological History

Previous reconstructions of Iran's ancient magmatic activity have largely centered on two major geological features: the Sananda-Sirjan Magmatic Arc and the Urumieh-Dokhtar Magmatic Arc.

The newly identified Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc adds another important piece to that history. Its discovery suggests that northwestern Iran experienced a separate episode of continental arc activity during the Late Cretaceous, expanding scientists' understanding of how the region developed.

The findings also point to a potentially important role for the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault. Researchers suggest that this fault may mark a major tectonic boundary connected to changes in the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean system.

Those changes may have included slab rollback, a process in which a descending tectonic plate retreats as it sinks into Earth's interior, as well as the migration of volcanic arcs to new locations. Such movements could help explain why this particular episode of magma formation lasted for a relatively short period.

New Clues About the Disappearance of an Ancient Ocean

Beyond Iran, the discovery provides a broader lesson about how Earth's geological history can become hidden over immense stretches of time.

Ancient magmatic arcs do not always survive as continuous, easily recognizable formations. Tectonic movements can break them apart, erosion can remove exposed rocks, and sedimentation can bury what remains. Later volcanic activity can further complicate the record, making older systems particularly difficult to identify.

By recognizing the surviving fragments of these ancient structures, scientists can better reconstruct how tectonic plates descended beneath one another, how volcanic arcs shifted, how continental crust grew, and how once-vast oceans eventually closed.

The Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc offers new evidence for understanding the Late Cretaceous evolution of northwestern Iran and the larger Neo-Tethyan region. It also helps researchers refine geological models of an area shaped by repeated episodes of ocean closure and continental collision.

The ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean played a major role in the geological development of the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Western Asia. Its eventual disappearance helped shape the modern landscapes of these regions.

By uncovering a volcanic system that had been largely erased from the geological record, researchers have added another piece to the complex story of how Earth's continents and oceans evolved over millions of years.

#718. Country Artists Who Have Been Voted Kennedy Center Honors (Full List)

This will mark the first time in the history of the Honors program that country artists have been recognized in back-to-back years.

When the Kennedy Center Honors are presented at Capital One Arena in downtown Washington, D.C. on Dec. 7, a country artist will be in the honors class for the second year in a row. Barbara Mandrell is being honored this year. George Strait was an honoree last year. This will mark the first time in the history of the Kennedy Center Honors that country artists have been recognized in back-to-back years.

Over the years, Mandrell has worked with several of the country artists who have received Kennedy Center Honors previously. George Jones, who received the honor in 2008, sang a guest vocal on Mandrell’s 1981 anthem “I Was Country When Country Wasn’t Cool.”

The Kennedy Center Honors program was slow to recognize country – as it was a lot of popular music forms. The first country artist to be honored was Roy Acuff  in 1991, in its 14th class of honorees.

The Kennedy Center Honors were first presented in 1978. The inaugural class consisted of contralto Marian Anderson, dancer-actor-singer Fred Astaire, choreographer George Balanchine, composer Richard Rodgers and pianist Arthur Rubinstein.

While the focus in the early years was on fine arts — heavy on classical and opera — over the decades, it has broadened to also include more popular forms of music. In 1987, B.B. King became the first blues artist to be inducted. Other performers who were the first in their genres to be honored were Acuff for country in 1991, Aretha Franklin for R&B in 1994, Pete Seeger for folk in 1994, Bob Dylan for rock in 1997, Gloria Estefan for Latin music in 2017 and LL Cool J for rap in 2017.

#717. Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch

Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising ability in immune cells that could reshape our understanding of how the body develops lasting protection against infections.

For years, researchers believed that tissue-resident memory T cells, specialized immune cells that remain in the body's tissues after an infection and respond quickly if the same threat returns, were guided mainly by chemical signals.

However, a new study published in Nature Immunology challenges that assumption. Researchers found that T cells can detect how stiff their surrounding tissues are and use this physical information to influence whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells. The findings suggest that adjusting to the stronger mechanical forces within tissues may be important for these protective cells to survive over time.

"This is an exciting fundamental finding that challenges the way we think about immune cells," said lead author Judith Mandl, a professor in McGill's Department of Physiology. "It suggests T cells can 'feel' their surroundings and adapt to them, making the physical environment an active force in shaping their behavior."

The research brought together scientists from McGill's Department of Physiology, the Alan Edwards Centre for Research on Pain, the Department of Bioengineering, and the McGill University Health Centre, along with collaborating institutions in the Netherlands and the United States.

How the Discovery Could Influence Cancer and Immune Treatments

Understanding how T cells respond to physical conditions could eventually open new possibilities for treating diseases in which the immune system mistakenly targets healthy tissue. These include autoimmune disorders, allergies, and complications involving transplant rejection.

The discovery could also have important implications for cancer research, particularly efforts to improve treatments that use the immune system to fight tumors.

"Tumors are often dense and physically difficult for immune cells to penetrate. Understanding how T cells adapt to these environments could help researchers design cancer immunotherapies that are better able to reach and attack tumors," said Mandl.

How Scientists Discovered the Immune Cells' Hidden Sense of Touch

To investigate whether physical surroundings influence T cell behavior, the researchers studied immune cells collected from humans and mice. They placed the cells inside specially designed collagen gels that mimicked tissues with different levels of stiffness.

The experiments revealed a clear pattern. As the gels became stiffer, T cells were increasingly likely to acquire characteristics associated with tissue-resident memory cells, which help provide long-term immune protection.

These results indicate that the physical properties of surrounding tissues can help shape how immune cells develop, adding an important new dimension to scientists' understanding of immune memory.

The researchers now hope to identify the specific molecular sensor that enables T cells to detect their physical environment. Determining how this sensor converts mechanical forces into changes in cell behavior could help explain how the immune system establishes lasting protection.

The study received funding from the Human Frontier Science Program, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Foundation for Innovation, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, and the U.S. National Institutes of Health.

#716. ‘Starlog’ Magazine Returns with First Cover in 17 Years

The publication, once a fixture of geek culture, will relaunch as an annual offering.

The last time there was a new edition of Starlog magazine, J.J. Abrams’ Star Trek was still weeks away from hitting theaters, Robert Downey Jr. was just scratching the surface of Tony Stark’s potential on the set of Iron Man 2, and George Lucas was still years away from selling Lucasfilm to Disney.

But 17 years after publishing its final issue in April 2009, Starlog is back with a new edition, which arrives Nov. 13.

The magazine launched in 1976 and gained a fanbase for being one of the few places to get reliable news and interviews about geek culture. It launched with a cover focusing on Star Trek, one of its key areas of expertise, but the magazine’s editors and writers also pioneered coverage of Star Wars. (The new issue chronicles some of the rumors it put out a year before the movie opened). In all, Starlog published 374 issues and more than 25,000 pages. Related Stories Lifestyle GQ Expands Men of the Year Footprint in L.A. Movies Cinemark Won't Screen Brad Pitt's 'Cliff Booth' Movie Over Netflix's Demands, CEO Says

The new iteration will publish one issue a year under editor in chief Annalee Newitz, a founding editor of io9. In addition to the film and TV-focused features Starlog was known for, the new Starlog will also delve into futurism, as the cover from Gabriel Yeganyan highlights. The opening story of issue No. 1 looks at the viability of humans farming crops on planets outside of Earth, for example.

“Science fiction and fantasy give us a sandbox to reimagine our world, and Starlog is your invitation to play along,” said Newitz in a statement. “We’re honoring the fannish legacy of the original magazine and bringing it into the future with hopeful, awe-inspiring, and scientifically grounded explorations of where humanity could go next.”

The revival was announced earlier this year, and includes a podcast hosted by Jordan Hoffman, a veteran journalist who has contributed to The Hollywood Reporter, as well as its weekly Lodestar newsletter. Fangoria Holdings, which also owns Fangoria and Gorezone, is behind the revival.

“During its original 33-year run, Starlog documented science fiction as it evolved across film,television, books, technology, and culture,” said co-owner Tara Ansley. “Fifty years after the magazine first launched, the line between science fiction and the real world has become increasingly difficult to separate. That makes this an especially interesting time to bring Starlog back. Technology may change, but the most compelling questions have always been about people: how we live, what we create, and what kind of future we want to build.”
